explanations.explanation: Maidens it is. She says, "No wonder the maidens adore you." The way I read it, his name is so well loved that the compliments show up before he does. That's a man whose cologne gets complimented before he's even parked the car.

I can see why elders came to mind, since an honored name sounds like something older folks would respect. But the verse says maidens, not elders. She says, "No wonder the maidens adore you." Sometimes the text just hands you the answer, so go with what it says.

No armor and no marching in this verse, friend. She says, "No wonder the maidens adore you." Soldiers never get a mention here. It's the maidens, and it's all about his name being like perfume poured out.

The king, right on the money. She says, "May the king bring me to his chambers." Notice she asks it in the same breath as "Take me away with you…" She's not asking for a map. She's asking to be taken.
Close in spirit, because a prophet is a big name. But no prophet shows up in this verse. She says, "May the king bring me to his chambers." The one she names is the king.
No priest in this verse, friend. She says, "May the king bring me to his chambers." A priest would have a whole other kind of room to bring her to, I bet. Here the word is king.

True. After all those "I" lines, the song says, "we will praise your love more than wine." It's like the whole room just joined the chorus. Funny how a solo can turn into a group number in half a verse.
It's actually true, friend. The text says, "we will praise your love more than wine." The song slides from "I" to "we" right there in verse 4. Same love, more voices singing about it.

explanations.answer: The sun has gazed upon her
explanations.explanation: The sun, yes. She says, "Do not stare because I am dark, for the sun has gazed upon me." The sun gets the credit, and she asks them not to stare. I think she's saying, "Okay, ladies, show's over."

explanations.answer: The smoke has settled on her
explanations.explanation: Smoke is a fun guess, but it's not in the verse. She says, "Do not stare because I am dark, for the sun has gazed upon me." The sun is what she names. No smoke, no soot, just sun.

explanations.answer: The wind has swept over her
explanations.explanation: The wind never comes up here. She says, "Do not stare because I am dark, for the sun has gazed upon me." It's the sun doing the gazing. The wind can sit this one out.
Vineyards. She says, "they made me a keeper of the vineyards…" Her mother's sons were angry with her, and that's the job they gave her. I think that's a lot of rows to look after.

Wells would be a job, sure, but this verse doesn't say wells. She says her mother's sons "…made me a keeper of the vineyards…" Notice she also mentions her own vineyard right after. Vineyards run all through that line.

Gates is a solid guard-duty guess, friend. But the verse says vineyards, not gates. She says they "…made me a keeper of the vineyards, but my own vineyard I have neglected." Both halves of that line are about vineyards.

explanations.answer: Like a veiled woman by his companions' flocks
explanations.explanation: That's the one. She asks, "Why should I be like a veiled woman beside the flocks of your companions?" She wants to find him instead of standing by somebody else's sheep. I think she's tired of guessing which flock is his.

explanations.answer: Like a stranger waiting at the city gate
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a believable line, but a city gate never comes up in this verse. She asks, "Why should I be like a veiled woman beside the flocks of your companions?" The picture is a woman standing by flocks. It's all pasture, no gate.

explanations.answer: Like a widow left alone in the field
explanations.explanation: No widow in this verse, friend. She asks, "Why should I be like a veiled woman beside the flocks of your companions?" The text says veiled woman, and it puts her beside the flocks. That's the picture she gives.
Shepherds. The answer comes back, "…graze your young goats near the tents of the shepherds." Follow the flock, find the tents. Sounds like a good plan for a girl with goats.

Merchants would have a lot of stuff to sell her, but this verse doesn't mention them. The line is "…graze your young goats near the tents of the shepherds." Goats and shepherds go together, so that tracks.

Travelers are a fair guess when someone's looking for directions. The verse says shepherds, though. The answer is "…graze your young goats near the tents of the shepherds." Travelers just aren't in that line.

This one is false, friend. The text has him say, "I compare you, my darling, to a mare among Pharaoh’s chariots." He calls her "my darling," and the very next verse says, "Your cheeks are beautiful with ornaments…" The text gives us no sign he's poking fun, and I think he's praising her.

False, and you read it right. He says, "I compare you, my darling, to a mare among Pharaoh’s chariots." The text gives him warm words for her, calling her "my darling" and then going on about her cheeks and neck. Nobody here is teasing.
Gold with silver beads. The verse says, "We will make you ornaments of gold, studded with beads of silver." It's a promise, and it's a shiny one. The "we" is back with something to say to her.

Linen and blue thread sound lovely, but they aren't in this verse. The promise is, "We will make you ornaments of gold, studded with beads of silver." It's ornaments, and they're gold and silver. Nothing woven in this one.

Bronze is a good metal, but it isn't the one named here. The verse says, "We will make you ornaments of gold, studded with beads of silver." Gold is the metal, and silver is the beads. No stones in that line.
Her perfume. She says, "While the king was at his table, my perfume spread its fragrance." The king is at his table, and her perfume is spreading its fragrance. I'd say she's getting noticed.
Incense is a nice smell, but this verse doesn't mention it. She says, "While the king was at his table, my perfume spread its fragrance." The fragrance is hers. Nothing from a temple is in this line.
No lamp oil in this verse, friend. She says, "While the king was at his table, my perfume spread its fragrance." It's her perfume doing the spreading. The lamps can stay lit without us.

True. She says, "My beloved is to me a cluster of henna blossoms in the vineyards of En-gedi." That's another picture for him, right after the sachet of myrrh. She's running out of ways to say it and not out of love.

It's true, friend. She says, "My beloved is to me a cluster of henna blossoms in the vineyards of En-gedi." Right after the sachet of myrrh, she gives him another picture. It's in the text word for word.
Handsome. She says, "How handsome you are, my beloved! Oh, how delightful!" He said beautiful, and she throws it right back to him. Nobody is leaving this conversation without a compliment.

Mighty is a strong word, but it isn't what she says. Her words are, "How handsome you are, my beloved! Oh, how delightful!" She's talking about how he looks and how delightful he is. Strength doesn't come up.
Gentle might be true of him, but this verse doesn't say it. She says, "How handsome you are, my beloved! Oh, how delightful!" The word she picks is handsome, and she follows it with delightful.

It's false, friend. The verse says, "The beams of our house are cedars; our rafters are fragrant firs." Gold does show up earlier, in the ornaments they promise her in verse 11. But the rafters are firs, and they smell good.
False, and nicely done. She says, "The beams of our house are cedars; our rafters are fragrant firs." Cedar beams and fir rafters, both fragrant woods. Gold is back in verse 11, as ornaments for her.

explanations.answer: She stands out from all the rest
explanations.explanation: She stands out. He says, "Like a lily among the thorns is my darling among the maidens." Thorns on one side and a lily on the other makes it easy to see who stands out. The picture puts her up against the other maidens, and she's the lily.

explanations.answer: She is quieter than all the rest
explanations.explanation: Quiet is a fair thing to read into a lily, but the verse doesn't say it. He says, "Like a lily among the thorns is my darling among the maidens." The picture is a lily against thorns. It's about how she stands out.

explanations.answer: She is younger than all the rest
explanations.explanation: The verse never says anything about age. He says, "Like a lily among the thorns is my darling among the maidens." It's the lily against the thorns that makes the point. She stands out from the rest.
Shade. She says, "I delight to sit in his shade, and his fruit is sweet to my taste." An apple tree gives you shade and fruit, and that's two gifts for one tree. I'd sit there too.
Branches are part of an apple tree, but they aren't what she names. She says, "I delight to sit in his shade…" Sitting in shade is a lot more comfortable than sitting on a branch.
Roots would be a lumpy seat, friend. The verse says, "I delight to sit in his shade…" The shade is where she sits, and the fruit is what she tastes.
Faint with love. She asks, "Sustain me with raisins; refresh me with apples, for I am faint with love." The text gives us the reason right there in her own words. I think she's got it bad.

explanations.answer: She is weary from the road
explanations.explanation: No road in this verse, friend. She says, "Sustain me with raisins; refresh me with apples, for I am faint with love." She tells us the reason herself. It's love that has her faint.

explanations.answer: She is weak from the heat
explanations.explanation: Heat makes sense with the sun mentioned earlier, but the verse gives a different reason. She says, "Sustain me with raisins; refresh me with apples, for I am faint with love." The text says love is why she's faint.
It's false, friend. She tells the daughters of Jerusalem, "Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right." That's the opposite of hurrying it along. She says wait for the right time.
False, you've got it. She says, "Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right." She doesn't tell them to rush anything. The timing matters to her, and she asks them to respect that.
